author: blu
body: A sync offer and its reply are BULK reconciliation: the asker offers everything it holds and the answerer sends back everything the offer did not name. These two are the opposite, and that is why they exist rather than reusing those. A quotation names one hash, so the ask is one hash and the answer is one work or nothing. The offer verb would have the asker publish its whole store to ask a single question, and the answerer serve its whole store to anyone who asked -- least authority in reverse.

author: blu
body: Locate is the question one layer above work-request: not "give me this work" but "who holds it". The two verbs stay separate because their answers are different kinds of thing. A work is content and is checkable by its own hash; an address is a hint and is checkable by nothing. Folding them into one verb would mean a registry had to hold every work it can point at, which is the entire cost the indirection exists to avoid.

author: blu
body: So a locate reply is worth exactly what a rumour is worth, and is treated that way: the asker still fetches by hash from whoever it names, and still checks what comes back against the hash it asked for. A registry that lies costs a wasted round trip and cannot cause a wrong work to be accepted. That is the argument that lets the transport be untrusted, applied one level further out.

author: blu
body: A peer tells a registry what it holds, so that a locate can be answered out of memory. This exists because the registry MUST NOT have to ask: answering a locate by probing peers means opening an outbound connection while an inbound one is still open, and a guest cannot do that -- the reply to the inbound connection is emitted and never delivered. Announcing inverts it. The peer dials at boot, when it has nothing inbound open, and the registry only ever accepts. The nesting is not avoided by careful sequencing; it becomes unreachable.

author: blu
body: An announcement is a rumour like a locate reply, and is worth the same: it says an address claims a digest. Nothing verifies the claim and nothing needs to, because the asker still fetches by hash and still checks what comes back. A peer that announces works it does not hold costs a wasted round trip.

author: blu
body: It goes stale by construction -- a peer can die or drop a work -- and that is affordable for the same reason. "Peer P holds digest D" is nearly monotonic, since a digest is immutable and the claim stays true until P goes away, and the fetch path already walks candidates in turn and tolerates a miss.
